Title: MCTFWC: a multiscale CNN-transformer fusion-based model for wound image classification

Abstract
Chronic wounds affect millions of individuals globally, creating substantial challenges for healthcare systems due to high
medical costs and the complexity of wound management. Accurate classiﬁcation of wound types is crucial for effective
diagnosis and treatment planning, enabling clinicians to determine optimal care procedures efﬁciently. However, most exist-
ing deep learning methods focus on binary classiﬁcation and struggle with multiclass wound classiﬁcation, particularly in
distinguishing complex wound types such as pressure and diabetic wounds. This study proposes a novel dual-branch archi-
tecture that combines a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Transformer to enhance wound classiﬁcation accuracy.
The CNN branch, based on a ResNet backbone, captures local features, while the Transformer branch, structured with a
pyramidal multi-scale design, encodes global contextual information at multiple resolutions. A Feature Fusion Attention
Block (FFAB) at each encoding level enhances feature integration through spatial and channel attention mechanisms. The
proposed model achieves superior performance in both binary and multiclass wound classiﬁcation, with average accuracies of
91.20% and 89.80%, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies conﬁrm the effectiveness of key
components, including the FFAB and parallelized CNN-Transformer structure. This work demonstrates the potential of the
proposed approach to signiﬁcantly improve diagnostic accuracy and efﬁciency, offering a robust solution for wound image
classiﬁcation in intelligent medical systems.
Keywords Wound image classiﬁcation · Convolutional neural networks · Vision transformers · Model fusion · Deep learning
1 Introduction
Wound formation can result from various factors, including
trauma (cuts, burns, deep lacerations), arterial and venous cir-
culation disorders, metabolic diseases, surgical procedures,
chronic ulcerations, and aging, which disrupt normal cellu-
lar behaviors and tissue repair processes [1]. The prevalence
of wounds is signiﬁcant, with diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs)
affecting about 34% of people with diabetes throughout
their lives [2]. Infection rates for DFUs are alarmingly high,
exceeding 50%. Venous leg ulcers (VLUs) are also preva-

suffering from active VLUs [3]. Pressure ulcers (PUs) pose
a signiﬁcant challenge, affecting 2.5 million people annually
[4]. Surgical wounds (SWs) are another common type, with
approximately 4.5% of individuals undergoing surgery each
year developing such wounds [5]. In-depth wound assess-
ment enhances patient outcomes by addressing psychosocial,
physical, and provider-patient dynamics, ultimately improv-
ing healing, quality of life, and satisfaction, and reducing
complications [6].
Traditional wound assessment methods are largely sub-
jective and experiential, leading to inconsistent therapeutic
strategies and challenges in delivering individualized care,
ultimately impacting patient outcomes negatively. Current
challenges in wound assessment and classiﬁcation include
subjective evaluation, limited classiﬁcation capabilities, and
the complexity of wound healing processes [7]. Advances
in technology, mainly through artiﬁcial intelligence (AI)
and Deep learning (DL), offer promising solutions to these
issues. Various imaging modalities are widely used in wound

imaging, such as Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) [8],
Infrared Thermography [9], Fluorescence Imaging [10], and
Digital Photography [11]. Among these modalities, standard
digital imaging combined with highly trained deep learn-
ing models can provide comprehensive overviews of wounds
with lower computational costs and simpler imaging setups.
Deep learning has emerged as a transformative approach
forwoundassessmentandclassiﬁcation,signiﬁcantlyenhanc-
ing accuracy and efﬁciency in clinical settings. Various
studies [11] have demonstrated the effectiveness of deep
learning models in categorizing different types of wounds,
thereby aiding healthcare professionals. These models can
classify multiple wound types, including venous, arterial,
pressure, deep, and infected wounds, using color images
captured by standard digital cameras. Traditional feature-
based machine learning methods, like those by Yadav et
al. [12] and Abubakar et al. [13], have been used for
wound classiﬁcation. Yadav et al. [12] employed color-based
feature extraction with SVM to classify grafted and non-
grafted wounds, while Abubakar et al. used pre-trained deep
architectures (ResNet101, VGG-face, ResNet152) for fea-
ture extraction and SVM for classiﬁcation. However, these
methods require manual parameter tuning, making them
time-intensive. In contrast, convolutional neural networks
(CNNs) automatically extract multiple layers of image fea-
tures without manual adjustments, improving efﬁciency.
Despite the success of CNNs in medical image analy-
sis, their application to wound classiﬁcation faces signiﬁcant
limitations. CNNs primarily focus on local spatial features
such as textures and edges but struggle to capture long-range
dependencies and global contextual information, which
are essential for distinguishing complex wound structures.
Meanwhile, Transformers process long-range dependencies
and global contextual information through self-attention
mechanisms. However, they lack inductive biases like spatial
locality and hierarchical feature learning, which makes them
less data-efﬁcient, especially when trained on limited medi-
cal datasets [14, 15]. While CNNs are limited by their lack
of global context and Transformers often miss ﬁne-grained
details, there is a gap in effectively combining these mod-
els to leverage their complementary strengths. This study
hypothesizes that a fusion-based approach integrating CNN
and Transformer can enhance feature representation, thereby
improving wound classiﬁcation accuracy, robustness, and
generalization across diverse wound types.
In this paper a parallelized multi-scale structure of CNN
and transformer with fusion block has been proposed for
wound classiﬁcation. The contributions of this study are bul-
leted below:
• Proposed a dual-branch parallel architecture integrat-
ing ResNet-based CNNs and a pyramidal Transformer
backbone to capture both local and global features for
enhanced wound image classiﬁcation.
• Developed a Feature Fusion Attention Block (FFAB) that
employs spatial and channel attention mechanisms for
effective feature fusion, ensuring superior semantic rep-
resentation.
• Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on binary and
multiclass wound classiﬁcation tasks, achieving notable
improvementsindiagnosticaccuracyandrobustnessover
existing models.
2 Literature
The exploration of fully automated techniques for segment-
ing wound tissues further emphasizes the potential of deep
learning in providing objective measurements that improve
clinical documentation accuracy. Recent advancements in
deep learning have signiﬁcantly transformed wound classi-
ﬁcation and assessment, showcasing a variety of innovative
approaches and methodologies. One notable study developed
a multi-modal network that integrates deep convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) with body location data to classify
wounds into categories such as diabetic, pressure, surgical,
and venous ulcers, achieving accuracy rates between 74.79%
and 100% utilizing architectures like VGG16, ResNet152,
and EfﬁcientNet [16]. Another research effort introduced a
deep learning-based tool to assist non-specialized medical
personnel in classifying ﬁve wound types (venous, arte-
rial, pressure, deep, and infected wounds), demonstrating
performance comparable to human experts through a multi-
task framework [17]. Goyal et al. [18] developed a deep
learning-based method to predict the presence of ischemia or
infection in diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) using a new dataset
of 1459 DFU images. The samples were augmented with
InceptionResNetV2 and Faster-RCNN networks, and binary
classiﬁcation experiments were conducted to categorize the
images into ischemia vs. non-ischemia and infection vs. non-
infection classes [18]. Additionally, they proposed DFUNet
structure incorporates both depth and parallel convolutional
layers to enhance the extraction of image features while
reducing the overall network depth. This design optimizes
the feature extraction process, and by reducing the number
of neurons in the fully connected layer, DFUNet is tailored
for a two-class classiﬁcation task, resulting in faster pro-
cessing times [19]. A novel architecture called Swish-ELU
EfﬁcientNet-B4 was proposed to enhance chronic wound
classiﬁcation accuracy while addressing class imbalance
issues [20]. Shenoy et al. [21] proposed a CNN-based method
for the binary classiﬁcation of wound images using a dataset
of 1335 images collected from the internet and smartphones.
The dataset included nine labels (drainage, granulation tis-
sue, infection, wound, ﬁbrinous exudates, sutures, staples,

four wound types and used a ﬁne-tuned AlexNet to design

classiﬁcation and 94.28% on average. For three-class classi-

The two-stage detection algorithm ﬁrst extracts regions of
interest (ROIs) from an image, then reﬁnes and classiﬁes
each ROI. R-CNN pioneered this approach but was slow due
to redundant feature extraction. Fast R-CNN improved efﬁ-
ciency with RoI pooling and a single feature extraction for the
whole image. Faster R-CNN further enhanced speed by inte-
gratingtheregionproposalnetwork(RPN)withFastR-CNN,
allowing region RoI detection, RoI’s feature extraction, and
classiﬁcation within one network [24]. Mask R-CNN [25]
extends Faster R-CNN by adding a predictive segmentation
mask. It replaces Faster R-CNN’s RoI pooling layer with an
RoI align layer, ensuring precise alignment of output pixels
with input pixels. This allows Mask R-CNN to perform both
object detection and segmentation with improved robustness
and speed. Recently, Mask R-CNN has been used to precisely
locate wounds in diabetic foot ulcers and determine wound
healing trajectories through visual and thermal image regis-
tration [26]. This approach holds promise for improving the
precisecharacterizationofwoundhealing,therebyadvancing
the understanding of wound progression in diabetic patients.
Yang et al. [27] explored the application of ViTs for skin
cancer classiﬁcation, which is relevant to wound classiﬁ-
cation, as ViTs enhance predictive accuracy and provide
explainable results through activation maps. Park et al. [28]
demonstrated the effectiveness of ViTs in surgical wound
classiﬁcation, achieving 92.78% accuracy, outperforming
other models in their study. Additionally, transformer-based
approaches for the early detection of oral cancer [29], blood
cell diagnosis [30], and skin lesion classiﬁcation [31] have
been explored, further highlighting the potential of trans-
formers in medical imaging. Several datasets are available
for wound classiﬁcation, each offering unique features for
researchandapplication.TheAZHMTDatasetincludes1088
images of various wound types-diabetic, pressure, surgical,
and arterial + venous leg ulcers [32]. Similarly, the AZH
Dataset comprises 730 images collected over two years at
the AZH Wound and Vascular Center, with detailed anno-
tations by wound specialists [32]. The Medetec Dataset
has another 358 images focusing on similar wound classes,
enhancing the overall dataset for classiﬁcation tasks [33].
For a broader scope, the ‘Deﬁned.ai Wound & Skin Image
Dataset’ features 100,800 images to detect skin diseases
and wounds, designed to improve AI diagnostics in health-
care [34]. Lastly, the Ensemble Deep CNN Dataset contains
538 images categorized into four wound types and is uti-
lized in studies involving ensemble deep learning techniques
[23]. Together, these datasets serve as valuable resources for
developing automated wound classiﬁcation systems using
deep learning. However, challenges remain, including data
scarcity, model generalization issues, and ensuring consistent
accuracy across diverse clinical settings and non-specialized
medical personnel, which necessitate robust evaluation met-
rics and ongoing research to ensure these technologies
effectively improve patient outcomes in wound care man-
agement.
3 Methodology
The advancement of deep learning lies in its ability to auto-
maticallyextractdeepfeaturesfromimagesforclassiﬁcation.
Unlike traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs),
which capture both global and local features across layers
and compress them into a fully connected layer for classiﬁ-
cation, the proposed model adopts a dual-branch structure.
This design extracts semantic information from input images
through two independent paths, enabling a more comprehen-
sive feature analysis. The proposed architecture integrates
parallel feature extraction using a CNN backbone (ResNet)
and Transformers, followed by a Feature Fusion Attention
Block (FFAB) at each encoding level, ultimately leading to
classiﬁcation. ResNet is employed for its robust representa-
tion of local features, while the Transformer branch utilizes a
pyramid structure to capture multi-resolution global informa-
tion effectively. ResNet provides an optimal balance between
efﬁciency, depth, and hierarchical feature extraction, making
it well-suited for the dual-branch architecture. The FFAB
at each level is key to enhancing the model’s performance.
It incorporates a channel and spatial attention mechanism,
ensuring an effective fusion of global and local features. This
enriched representation improves the model’s ability to dis-
cern meaningful patterns for accurate classiﬁcation. At the
classiﬁcation stage, a hierarchical representation of the fused
features are processed by an inverted residual MLP-based

3.1 Parallelized feature
Inspired by the previously mentioned CNN and transformer-
based classiﬁcation model, a parallelized feature extraction
approach is introduced to capture both global and local
information from images for classiﬁcation. This approach
employs three distinct stages to extract diverse and compre-
hensive features effectively. By operating at different scales,
it ensures the integration of varied perspectives, enhancing
the model’s ability to analyse intricate patterns in images.
The multi-scale feature extraction strategy enriches the clas-
siﬁcation process by leveraging complementary information
across parallel stages.
3.1.1 Pyramidical transformer backbone
Transformers, originally developed for natural language pro-
cessing (NLP), have been successfully adapted to computer
vision, delivering remarkable results in classiﬁcation tasks.
By dividing an image into sequences of patches, ﬂatten-
ing them, and processing them through multiple transformer
blocks, these models achieve performance comparable to
convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Building on this, a
pyramidal structure is proposed to generate multi-scale fea-
ture maps, leveraging a three-stage parallelized transformer
architecture. Unlike the standard ViT, which maintains a
ﬁxed resolution, the pyramid-based approach progressively
reduces spatial dimensions while increasing channel depth,
mimicking CNNs to capture both ﬁne-grained local details
and global contextual information. Multi-scale extraction
processes features at different receptive ﬁelds, ensuring both
local textures and global structures contribute to classiﬁ-
cation. Each stage includes a patch embedding layer and
a transformer layer to process the features effectively. In
the proposed structure, In ﬁrst stage of Transformer back-
bone an input image of size H × W × 3 is divided into
patches by a patch embedding layer with a patch size of 4.

3.1.2 CNN backbone
The parallel branch of the Transformer backbone employs
a CNN backbone, utilizing ResNet to capture local infor-
mation ﬂow at different hierarchical levels of the image.
ResNet incorporates the concept of residual learning, which
determines the difference between the input vector and the
learned feature vector. To align feature map sizes with
the Transformer, image features are progressively down-
sampled by factors of 4, 8, and 16 using ResNet layers.
At each stage, a convolution layer and a downsampling
operation are performed, resulting in three feature maps:
{FC N N_1, FC N N_2, FC N N_3}. These feature maps,
generated at distinct stages of the CNN backbone, encapsu-
late essential spatial information at varying scales, providing
a local representation for downstream processing in proposed
models. This hierarchical feature extraction facilitates effec-
tive integration of local and global image features, enhancing
the model’s overall ability to process and understand com-
plex visual patterns.

3.2 Feature fusion attention block
The Feature Fusion Attention Block (FFAB) is utilized in
each stage to combine feature maps from the Transformer
and CNN backbones with semantic information from the pre-
vious stage. This enables effective fusion of signiﬁcant local
and global features, passing them from parallel backbone net-
works to the classiﬁer, facilitating skin lesion classiﬁcation
in wound images. Unlike traditional convolution-based fea-
ture combining, the FFAB employs channel-wise fusion to
emphasize semantically relevant features while suppressing
irrelevant ones, ensuring efﬁcient integration of global and
local information. At each stage, spatial attention is applied
to CNN feature maps FC N N_i ∈RHi×W i×Ci , focusing on
critical regions by computing an attention map. The attention
map Aspatial is then applied to the original CNN features by
element-wise multiplication to focus on the regions that the
attention mechanism deems more important.

4 Experimental settings
4.1 Datasets
In this study, we evaluated the proposed model using two
publicly available datasets.
Dataset 1 is derived from Rostami et al. [23] over the
two year collection from the two wound and vascular care,
namely the AZH Wound and Vascular Center in Milwaukee,
Wisconsin, and images were labelled by a wound special-
ist from the AZH Wound and Vascular Center. The dataset
consists of 400 wound images in JPG format, with varying
dimensions ranging from 240 × 320 to 525 × 700 pixels
and a bit depth of 24. These images represent four wound
types-venous, diabetic, pressure, and surgical-each category
comprising 100 images, ensuring a balanced dataset. The
images were captured using a Canon SX 620 HS digital cam-
era and an iPad Pro. Most of the images in the dataset were
sourced from individual patients; however, a few instances
include multiple images of the same patient, taken from dif-
ferent body sites or during various healing stages. The dataset
has also included ROI images that target the wound area in
whole images. Both whole images and ROI images have been
used to evaluate the classiﬁcation performance.
Dataset 2 has been derived from the study conducted
by the Oota et al. [35] The dataset was collected from Jun
2015–Mar2019withthewoundspecialistperformstheanno-
tation and labelling. The dataset is highly diverse, featuring
images of eight types of wound ulcers, including trauma,
surgical, venous, diabetic, cellulitis, arterial, pressure, and
others. We only included diabetic (D), pressure (P), trauma
(T),venous(V)andsurgical(S)asitismajorclassesinwound
and hard to classify. These wound types represent the most
prevalent and diagnostically challenging categories, requir-
ing advanced feature extraction and classiﬁcation techniques.
4.2 Implementation details
Each dataset is trained with batch size of 8 for 100 epochs.
The datasets were split into train, valid and test as stan-
dard 70%, 15% and 15% ratio. The images were resized to
224×224, normalized, and subjected to standard augmenta-
tions for training. The robust accuracy reported was obtained
by 5-fold cross validation. The cross validation include a set
of four folds for training and 5th fold for validation. The aver-
age of accuracy is reported as the ﬁnal accuracy. We utilized
the AdamW optimizer that adapts learning rates dynamically
while incorporating weight decay for better generalization,
ensuring effective training by adjusting learning rates based
on gradient changes with a initial learning rate 1 × 10−4.
To evaluate the performance, we evaluated the deep learn-
ing performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall
and F1 score. Also, the ROC curve has been plotted to see

and low-frequency guided CNN network (HLG-NET) for
wound classiﬁcation, also evaluated on the AZH dataset.
Their reported binary classiﬁcation accuracies for DP, PS,
and SV were 84.62%, 88.89%, and 98.0%, respectively. For
DPS, PSV, and DPSV classiﬁcation, their reported accura-
cies were 74.19%, 88.06%, and 82.61%, respectively. While
HLG-NET demonstrates better performance in certain binary
classiﬁcation tasks, our proposed method outperforms it
in three- and four-class classiﬁcations. This highlights the
strength of our approach, particularly in handling higher-

success. Our ﬁndings align with comparisons to other state-
of-the-art classiﬁcation models, reinforcing the effectiveness

increasing computational complexity and slowing down both

6 Conclusion
In this article, we introduced a novel method for the classi-
ﬁcation of wound images and wound patches using publicly
available datasets, covering a range of classiﬁcation tasks
from binary to multiclass classiﬁcation. Our model lever-
ages a pretrained CNN backbone, a transformer block, and
a Feature Fusion Attention Block (FFAB) to effectively
integrate critical local and global features. This enriched
feature representation, processed through parallel backbone
networks, enhances the model’s ability to achieve accurate
and efﬁcient skin lesion classiﬁcation in wound images. The
proposed approach signiﬁcantly outperforms recent state-of-
the-art models, achieving an average accuracy for multiclass
classiﬁcation is 89.80% reported. The results highlight the
robustness and effectiveness of the proposed architecture in
advancing automated wound image analysis.
The domain of chronic wound classiﬁcation faces a
scarcity of publicly available datasets, particularly for multi-
class classiﬁcation, with existing datasets offering limited
samples. Future efforts should focus on creating larger and
more diverse public datasets while focusing on develop-
ing robust and generalized deep learning models to improve
performance, especially in cross-corpora evaluations. Addi-
tionally, future research plans include exploring the effective
feature fusion of CNNs and Transformers to enhance skin
lesion image analysis.

Abstract: Chronic wounds affect millions of individuals globally, creating substantial challenges for healthcare systems due to high medical costs and the complexity of wound management. Accurate classiﬁcation of wound types is crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment planning, enabling clinicians to determine optimal care procedures efﬁciently. However, most exist- ing deep learning methods focus on binary classiﬁcation and struggle with multiclass wound classiﬁcation, particularly in distinguishing complex wound types such as pressure and diabetic wounds. This study proposes a novel dual-branch archi- tecture that combines a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Transformer to enhance wound classiﬁcation accuracy. The CNN branch, based on a ResNet backbone, captures local features, while the Transformer branch, structured with a pyramidal multi-scale design, encodes global contextual information at multiple resolutions. A Feature Fusion Attention Block (FFAB) at each encoding level enhances feature integration through spatial and channel attention mechanisms. The proposed model achieves superior performance in both binary and multiclass wound classiﬁcation, with average accuracies of 91.20% and 89.80%, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies conﬁrm the effectiveness of key components, including the FFAB and parallelized CNN-Transformer structure. This work demonstrates the potential of the proposed approach to signiﬁcantly improve diagnostic accuracy and efﬁciency, offering a robust solution for wound image classiﬁcation in intelligent medical systems.
